name: Extended SMAS facelift

card.summary: A facelift that lifts the SMAS layer and extends the dissection forward over the cheek to reposition sagging midface fat, soften nasolabial folds and sharpen the jawline.
card.note: Major surgery under anesthesia; risks include hematoma, facial nerve injury and scarring.

quick.overview:
The extended SMAS facelift lifts the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), the fibrous layer beneath facial skin, and extends the dissection further forward than a standard SMAS lift. A review describes it as targeting two cardinal signs of aging: descent of malar (cheek) fat, which deepens nasolabial folds and tear troughs, and jowls that blur the lower jawline.[1]

The appearance payoff is a lifted midface, a more defined jaw and neck, and softer folds. Standard SMAS plication and imbrication improve the lower face and neck but give little lifting effect at the midface, which the extended technique was designed to address.[5]
quick.how: It is performed by a plastic surgeon under general anesthesia or sedation, with incisions near the ear and hairline. The SMAS is elevated and repositioned in a different vector than the skin, and the technique is often combined with neck work such as submentoplasty.[2] Wikipedia lists a traditional facelift recovery of about three to four weeks.[6]
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists hematoma as the most common complication, followed by temporary or permanent nerve injury, scarring, hair loss near incisions, earlobe distortion and, rarely, infection; smoking raises skin necrosis risk.[6] In a comparative study, temporary buccal branch facial nerve weakness occurred in two patients.[4] Surgeons discuss retaining ligaments and plane choice as technical trade-offs.[3]

lead: The extended SMAS facelift is a rhytidectomy technique in which the SMAS is elevated together with a wider area of cheek tissue, extending dissection past the standard lateral SMAS flap to lift the malar fat pad and the nasolabial region.[1] It is one of several SMAS-based methods developed after Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS in 1976.[6]

Its stated goals are to correct malar fat descent, which deepens the nasolabial folds and tear trough, and to improve jowls that obscure the lower jaw border.[1] Surgeons also use a modified deep plane extended SMAS with submentoplasty for the neck, reporting significant lasting improvement.[2]

Published literature includes a randomized comparison of lateral, standard, extended SMAS and composite rhytidectomies,[4] narrative reviews on facelift techniques,[5][3] and a description of the extended SMAS approach in Asian patients.[8]

chain: Dissect and elevate the SMAS forward over the cheek
Reposition descended malar fat and jowl tissue
Fuller midface, softer nasolabial fold, cleaner jaw and neck
angle.text: The operation repositions the deeper tissue layer so the cheeks sit higher and the jawline is better defined, rather than only tightening skin.

infobox: About 3-4 weeks for a traditional facelift[6]
SMAS plication, deep plane, composite, multiplane[7]

paras: Facelift techniques are classified by the depth and extent of dissection. Plication and imbrication SMAS lifts are the classical methods, but a review notes they have no lifting effect at the midface level.[5] The extended SMAS addresses the midface and jowls by dissecting further forward and releasing deeper attachments.[1]

The multiplane facelift is described as a fourth-generation rhytidectomy that combines features of the extended SMAS and deep-plane lifts, aiming to treat the nasolabial fold with bidirectional pull and a longer-lasting result.[7]

Wikipedia notes that Holländer reportedly performed the first facelift in 1901, that Skoog introduced subfacial dissection, and that Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS in 1976, after which SMAS-based surgery became standard.[6] A Clinics in Plastic Surgery review gives a short history of the extended SMAS operation and landmark papers.[1]

A 1996 randomized comparison at a New York hospital studied 21 patients, almost all women with a mean age of 59, with different procedures on each side of the face: extended SMAS or composite against limited or conventional SMAS, with photographs reviewed by three surgeons.[4] Complications were few, with temporary buccal branch weakness in two patients.[4]

A 1994 paper argues for renewed interest in the superficial-plane approach as a safe alternative to deep-plane, extended SMAS, subperiosteal and composite methods, reporting experience in 750 patients.[9]
A 2025 review examines how techniques handle facial retaining ligaments and notes debate about preserving versus releasing them.[3]
Complications listed by Wikipedia for facelifts include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (especially in smokers), scarring and hair loss near incisions.[6]

A prospective randomized comparison of lateral, standard and extended SMAS and composite facelifts (21 patients, one-year follow-up) is the main controlled study.[4] Other literature consists of technique descriptions and narrative reviews.[1][2][3][5][8]

timeline.event: Eugen Holländer reportedly performs an early facelift in Berlin.[6]
Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS.[6]
Multiplane facelift and superficial-plane revisit papers published.[7][9]
Randomized comparison of SMAS facelift types published.[4]
